utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, good afternoon to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you, too. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to my learned friends from the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, I am here together with Gramsci Di Fazio, co-counsel, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you and your team. And appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, my name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with John Jones I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts, and our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. So, Madam Registrar, you would have noticed that we started an hour and a couple of minutes later than scheduled, and that's because of -- we were concluding all that needed to be done before the sitting. I would like you to start keeping a note starting from today - you and whoever might replace you - of any time lost, and we will then tell you -- you will bring that to our attention and we will tell you to credit it to the Defence time. The time started from 2.15, and it continues until we conclude the matters that we are going to finish. All right. So the first thing that I wanted to announce is that a few minutes ago we filed our written decision on the Defence filings following the scheduling order that we discussed, which I don't know whether you have been given a copy as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'll make sure that you will be given a copy. More or less -- I mean, it's what we anticipated of course last Friday, except for one thing that -- I'll be coming to this, but having looked at your motion for certification, you're asking for certification of our oral decision. What we did last Friday was not an oral decision; it was the anticipation of what - we made it clear - was going to be a written decision. So it's not the end of the world. It's something which is not of significance. Before we clear up the matter of certification, since this is being filed well within the seven-day period, I want to know whether you are going to stay silent on this or whether you want time to file a reply because if you do not require any time to file a reply or you're prepared to make submissions now or prefer to stay silent, then we can proceed with our decision, which will be oral now; we're giving you an indication of what we're going to decide, to be followed by a written decision later on in the day at the end of the day, before the closing time of registry. Yes, Mr. Wubben, don't make our lives difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to submit that we will not oppose it and we will not give a written reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and I really appreciate that, Mr. Wubben. I told the two colleagues that I had no doubt that this is what I would have -- I would hear from your mouth. So later on we will be handing down a written decision, granting certification. I can also tell you as from now that in the concluding part of the decision granting certification we are also drawing the attention of the Appeals Chamber to the urgent need to have this matter decided as early as possible. So that is for your information. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply to explain, Your Honour, the reason why we filed a request for certification on the basis of the oral decision, as we characterised it, was two-fold: One, to preserve our decision because we didn't want to start the Defence case without already setting in train an appeal; and secondly, because as you will see, we are also applying for a stay, again more formally than we did on Friday, and it didn't seem to make sense to file a stay of proceedings pending appeal unless we had initiated the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully understand, Mr. Jones. What I want you to do, unless you find objection to doing it, is please make a short statement now that following my declaration that there was no such oral decision but a written decision, that your motion applies to the written decision -- same arguments apply to the written decision, and that will be your motion for all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I can orally make that declaration or motion and adopt the words which Your Honour has just outlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Which brings us to the next problem, and that rises in the wake of the second motion that was filed by the Defence, namely that of the staying of proceedings pending the outcome of the appeal on the decision we have just -- the written decision that we have just filed a few minutes ago. Again, I don't think it's the case of requiring from the Defence any elaboration on the arguments that are adduced in that motion. And what I would like to know is whether the Prosecution would like to take a position on that motion and whether they are in a position to take that position today rather than ask for -- not ask for time, it's a right that you have -- than avail yourself of the time that you have, according to our Rules, to reply in writing to that motion. I can tell you what our preference is. Our preference is, obviously, that you do not, if possible, avail yourself of that possibility and that you provide us with your remarks or your response orally now if you are going to respond in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will do so. And given the very extraordinary circumstances of the case and also by supporting the expeditious way to handle issues like this, any delay of the procedure, as of course the concern of the OTP. So in that respect, I would like to limit that part of the issue of the request to that specific comment by us because a delay will mean that precious time is wasted -- and I don't mean wasted in a negative way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Used -- not used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Lost. Thank you, Your Honour, much obliged. It will be lost and that's why it has the concern of the OTP. The alternative proposal in the motion is therefore -- sounds more reasonable whenever it comes to a confirmation or a denial by the Appeals Chamber later on, and that will not take into account. So rather, in that -- given those circumstances and the argumentation, I would prefer a supporting of the alternative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which alternative --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: At the end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 18. But your -- let's take it. The Defence in the Defence in the first place requests the Trial Chamber to re-consider its position and to order a stay of proceedings pending the hearing of the appeal, which would also give the Defence adequate time to re-consider its position in the light of the Trial Chamber's decision on the length of time. This is part of the accused's fundamental right. Then in the alternative the Defence requests the Trial Chamber not to count the two weeks and four witnesses called in July 2005 as part of the nine weeks and 30 witnesses allocated for the Defence to present its case, and therefore to reschedule the close of the Defence case accordingly. Are you telling me that out of these two requests of the -- of the Defence you would rather have us decide in favour of the second rather than of the first?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and not in such a way that I would plead to allow the second alternative, but I am rather opposing a first and in favour of the second than the other way around. So that's my -- that's my oral position at this time, and I would like to confirm that in one of the two coming days, in short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically what you are saying is that instead of giving the Defence nine weeks, we would be giving them 11 weeks. And instead of 30 witnesses, we would be giving them 33 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you that I would -- I would rather -- I would rather be -- if any preference given by choice by those two, it will be the second; but with a view of the second I would like to confirm that in written reply within one of the two coming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the meantime we have to decide today whether we stay the proceedings today and whether we continue. I have got one witness here already in the corridor; I saw her being escorted to the room. I suppose that Mr. Jones already has the next witness present here in The Hague. So if we -- I can't stop you for asking for time, but I do plead with you, if possible, to give us an answer here and now because we have got at least two witnesses that I know of present here in The Hague. I don't know if the third one is present here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at least we have got two here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I oppose any delay, any stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I just briefly, Your Honour. I won't, of course, outline the reasons for our application for stay because Your Honour has them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, they are very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply for the public that are following, we say that in the dramatic developments of receiving directions last week we need firstly time to get our house in order and we need in particular to avoid calling witnesses that may not be necessary and thereby wasting four witnesses and two weeks out of nine weeks and 30 witnesses. And we say there's no compelling reason why the next two weeks -- why we need to sit those two weeks. If I might respond to Your Honour's observation, a practical one, that there are two witnesses in The Hague, that of course there's a point of principle here for us, that at the same time those two witnesses are here and one conceivable approach might be that we sit this week with those witnesses and a stay -- it would be appropriate as of the start of next week. That's one possible suggestion. And then just briefly on the difference -- or the alternative in paragraph 18 of not counting the extra -- these two weeks. In effect, I think it comes in some ways to the same thing, because the Appeals Chamber will presumably give a ruling within four to six weeks in any event by the time we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't guarantee anything on behalf of the Appeals Chamber. I can assure you of one thing, and you know as much about this as we do, we know probably a little bit than you do, the Appeals Chamber in its various compositions is very heavily burdened at the moment, and that is precisely why I have precisely -- because usually we wouldn't conclude in a decision an exhortation to the Appeals Chamber to give priority to this appeal rather than others. But I think that I can safely - and we've discussed this at length - we can safely take the liberty of addressing the Appeals Chamber in that direction, but then of course it's up to the Appeals Chamber to regulate its own scheduling, with obviously we cannot interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that -- I won't make any guesses in that respect then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But the alternative proposal that the weeks and witnesses not be counted against us is really a device whereby that any prejudice against us is removed because that way we have these two weeks free in essence and it doesn't count against us. So that's the reason for that request for alternative relief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we would like to make clear is the following, that the fact that you have two witnesses here already here in The Hague and prepared to start giving evidence is an argument in your favour and not being used as an argument against. In fact, it would have been used as an argument against you if you had come forward and said, We insist on this stay of proceedings and we are not calling these first two witnesses to be present here in The Hague, et cetera. So it's the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're forced to call them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the kind of behaviour that we would expect from a reasonable and respectful Defence team in any case. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's decide this orally and if you so require we will follow up with a written decision. We hope that you will not require it after that you've heard what we have to say. We are deciding orally the motion filed earlier on today by the Defence for Naser Oric called "Urgent Defence Motion For a Stay of Proceedings Pending Appeal." The Trial Chamber is deciding this motion orally now, after having confirmed to the parties its intention to grant by means of a written decision certification granting leave for appeal of the decision, written decision, which I referred to earlier on on the two Defence filings following the schedule order we issued some time back. What we are going to decide now is whether the Trial Chamber should stay the proceedings or not. There are two alternatives that are being put forward by the Defence in the motion. The first one is that the Trial Chamber reconsiders it position and order a stay of proceedings, pending the hearing of the appeal, which would also give the Defence adequate time to reconsider its position in the light of the Trial Chamber's decision on the length of time. The alternative remedy that is being sought by the Defence is that the Trial Chamber not count the two weeks and four witnesses that would be called in July 2005 as part of the nine weeks and 30 witnesses allocated for the Defence to present its case, and therefore to reschedule the close of the Defence case accordingly. The Trial Chamber, having heard -- having gone through the reasons brought forward in this motion and also we've heard what the Prosecution had to say, does not agree either that it should reconsider its position and order a stay of proceedings pending the hearing of the appeal, and as well as not to count the two weeks and four witnesses called in this month as part of the nine weeks and 30 witnesses allocated for the Defence to present its case. The reasons are as follows: Primarily it's because we consider that the reasons adduced in this motion in support of the two requests, although of course they carry some weight, however they do not -- they are not of enough significance in this eyes of the Trial Chamber such as to outweigh the interests of justice that the -- that the Trial Chamber considers as necessary in the present circumstances in order to be able to proceed with the case and commence the Defence case. In other words, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these are not vexatious or superfluous reasons that have been given, but they are not enough to outweigh the interests of justice to continue with the case. That is the primary consideration that we have. Also underlying this decision is the fact that although we hope the Appeals Chamber will hand down its decision, preferably -- I mean, I say it without hesitation, but as I say I cannot -- I have no control on these issues, on these matters, preferably before the end of the summer recess so that you will know in the meantime what the situation is and the Prosecution will know, and we in particular would know. Still, there is no guarantee that we will get this before August 15th. So a request to order a stay of proceedings pending the hearing and determination of the appeal not knowing when the appeal is going to finish might entail a decision which would mean the staying of proceedings also beyond the summer recess, and we don't think that that is what we ought to do. The other alternative, we have the following to say: We have requested the Defence to bring forward four witnesses or enough witnesses to fill in the two weeks that we have starting from today until the end -- until the summer recess, the two weeks that we agreed upon. We do appreciate that you could have difficulty in identifying a fourth or a fifth witness to bring over, considering the relative short time that you've had. We do not agree that you should encounter also such problems in relation to the first three witnesses, that is Madam Edina, who is waiting outside, and the other two witnesses, Redzic and Dachy. As regards the fourth witness, we trust judge in your good judgement and sense of cooperation, and we believe that if you are in a position to bring that person - I won't mention the name because I don't know if he will be protected or not - the fourth person that we have got on the list today, that if you are in a position to bring him over, you bring him over. What we can promise you is the following, Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic, if there is any remaining time after we finish with that evidence at the 15th of July that we agreed upon, then that will be a credit. We will stop, we will not force you to bring any witnesses, those remaining, one, two, three, I don't know, we will not force you, but please do make your utmost to bring the fourth witness if you can. I mean, I know that you are responsible enough not to play games, and I take your word that you won't. But it is important for us not to lose time as much as we can. All right. So that is the position. If you end up on the second week with your back to the wall and we are satisfied that you did your best and you found -- you encountered difficulties, you are not going to find us unreasonable. I don't think we have ever been unreasonable with you, even though you think we are unreasonable with you now. Time will prove to you that we weren't. But this is the position. So that is our decision. If you require it in writing, we will hand it down in writing and then we'll see what the situation will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Two matters really. We are doing our utmost to have that witness there, the fourth witness, and I trust that we will be able to bring him here. We certainly don't require that decision in writing. On the other hand, I wonder if Your Honours could certify that matter also for appeal so that that can be included globally in the appeal which we will be bringing. In some ways it might be academic, because by the time the Appeals Chamber rules on the matter, it might be too late for the stay to be granted. But it is a matter which, it seems, falls within the context of our complaint and therefore should be reviewed by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think is this: I want to consider one thing, Mr. Jones, that this is an area which is not virgin ground, whether or not there should or should not be a stay of proceedings pending the determination of appeals. And I suppose I don't need to go into the case for that exists. I very much suspect that if we were to give you this opportunity, that you would include it in your appeal, it may influence the Appeals Chamber in the preliminary filtering process that takes place of whether to go ahead with the appeal or not. My suggestion to you is as follows: It will be difficult for us to certify it, simply because the case law of this Tribunal is constantly against staying proceedings pending the outcome of appeals decisions, except of course when it is absolutely unavoidable, which is not the case I think. And if we do certify it, I mean you would be trying to tie -- or rather, we would be trying to tie the hands of the Appeals Chamber to decide an issue with extreme urgency, when we could have decided it definitively for ourselves and not grant certification. I mean -- I don't know what else -- I don't know what I -- I think you should be reading my mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I hear what Your Honour says, and it may be a matter of simply declining certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we decline certification. I think it's wiser, and it pays you more not to insist on the Appeals Chamber and throw this in their lap --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We don't want them to rush in their decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They won't rush in their decision; they'll throw it back to you. I don't think that it's wise on your part to play it that way. I shouldn't be saying all this, but in actual fact I do want to convince you that I have the best interest of your client at heart as well as that of the overall interests of justice. So that having been said, Madam Registrar, I want you to log the time that we have spent starting from 2.15 until now -- yes, I recognise Mr. Wubben is going to take more of your time, Mr. Jones. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, though it will be very short because this is the first opportunity I have to address before an imminent start of the Defence case of hearing the witnesses. With a view to the Rule 98 bis ruling by this Trial Chamber, I would like to put on the record that the Prosecution did not appeal this 98 bis ruling of the Trial Chamber, in particular with a view to the part of the decision regarding the counts of plunder. We did not appeal, though we did not agree by itself with the considerations of the Trial Chamber to come to that conclusion of -- regarding the plunder. The reason for not appealing by the OTP is the specific circumstances and background with a view to the issues involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you. And indeed I do want to make myself clear because this has been in the back of my mind all the time since we wrote that special conclusory part in the Rule 98 bis decision, inviting you to consider amending the indictment according -- to reflect the Rule 98 bis decision. We were careful to choose the word -- we didn't order, we invited you. At the same time, fully cognizant of the usual cooperation we find from parties, certainly also from the Prosecution. I did not want you for a moment to think that by asking you, for example, count number 4, leave it there and put deleted in brackets, count number 6, leave it is there and put deleted in brackets, we were asking you to make a declaration that would prejudice your rights to appeal at a later point in time which goes against you. So that is the position. So please do take it for granted that we did not in any way try to prejudice your rights and you should not consider your rights prejudiced. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Right. Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it is up to the Appeals Chamber, if there is an appeal from you, to consider whether you have prejudiced them or not but it was not our intention to provide you or trick you into a position where you would prejudice your right to appeal. All right. Yes, your first witness, Mr. Jones, or Madam Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We, I'm dealing with this witness. May I just say that obviously we gave an opening speech at the start of the entire trial on the 6th of October, 2004, so for the record, again, for the public who are following this, that's the opening speech of the Defence in this case and we don't have a right to make one now, and we are not proposing to make one. So we would simply call our first witness, Edina Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your client doesn't wish to make any statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I do appreciate that, in fact we had dealt with this last day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this should be very brief, this next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Madam Becirevic, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whose microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Madam Becirevic, could I kindly ask you to raise your voice a little bit when you answer because the fact that you are standing up, you are distant from the microphones and you're not being heard by the interpreters. So I welcome you once more to the Trial Chamber. You are about to start giving evidence as the first witness for the Defence in this case against Naser Oric. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence you enter a declaration, a solemn declaration, to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher will be handing you a -- the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be testifying the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Please take a chair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones will be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apologies, Witness, that you were kept waiting while we dealt with administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I join in that. We had several administrative matters to deal with and in a way we are lucky to have dealt with them since we start. Madam Registrar, have you logged in the time 2.15 until 10 to 4.00, please. That's the time to be recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I need to know when we are to break. Write it down on a piece of paper when we need to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Witness, if you can keep your voice up as much as possible, and you can address your answers to the Bench. Even though I'm asking the questions Their Honours, you can answer towards Their Honours. Now, first of all, can you please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Edina Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your date of birth, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The 27th of January, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your nationality?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that your first language is B/C/S or Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Becirevic, if at any time -- I take it that since I was speaking in English and you were replying that you are receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time there are problems with interpretation -- I mean, either you're not receiving it or else the volume is too high or too loud, then please do tell us straight away and we'll take the necessary steps to rectify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, sorry for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As well as Bosnian you speak and understand English?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I won't ask you for a full curriculum vitae, but if you could start by telling us a little bit about your academic and professional qualifications. First of all, what are your academic qualifications?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I am now working on a PhD at the faculty of political sciences in Sarajevo. I have a Masters Degree from the London School of Economics in media communications. I studied at the social psychology department in 1967 [as interpreted]. I also have a Masters Degree in the political sciences from the Central European University in Budapest. In Sarajevo I graduated in journalism at the faculty of political sciences in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. We might need to enter one correction in the record. When in fact did you study at the social psychology department -- the record says 1967, which must be a bit too early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can't be 1967. I was there in 1964, so -- I don't remember Madam Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If it's of any assistance to the Defence, if Your Honours, please, I've got no objection to Mr. Jones leading throughout all this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If there is any problem, I'll let Mr. Jones know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Jones, that will make your life easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, but in this case I can't lead the date because I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do put to the witness when she is supposed to be studying at the LSE.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me take it from the top. First, is it right that you have a degree in political science and journalism?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in 1989 in Sarajevo. I apologise about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you also have degrees from the London School of Economics and from the Central European University in Budapest?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. From 1993 to 1996 I did a postgraduate degree at the London School of Economics, and in 2000 and 2001 at the Central European University in Budapest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it right that you worked as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a journalist until four years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you just very briefly outline what some of your activities and responsibilities were as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was she a freelance journalist or was she a journalist attached to a particular -- employed by a particular newspaper or TV or radio station?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that would be more important for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For about ten years, I worked partly as a freelance journalist and at certain periods of time I worked for foreign television stations. For example, during the war in Sarajevo I worked for WTN, Worldwide Television News. After the war, I worked for Slobodna Bosna as a journalist. I also worked as a freelancer for numerous local Bosnian and Herzegovinian television stations and for some -- or rather, various newspapers throughout the former Yugoslavia. So part of the time I worked as a freelancer and part of the time I had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. contracts with various television stations or various magazines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And what's your current occupation or your current occupations?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Currently I am a hired assistant at the Faculty of Criminal Sciences in Sarajevo in national security and I'm also a lecturer at the Maryland university at their department in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you also, are you not [Realtime transcript read in error "not"], an investigator in the office of Vasvija Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I am an investigator in Ms. Vasvija Vidovic's office, working on the Oric case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that was since 2003 more or less. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what are some of your duties there if you can just explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, because we have got a mistake. Line 15 of page -- we've got a mistake in the transcript. Line 15 your question was put done: And are you also not an investigator in the office of Vasvija Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's rhetorical English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In any event, you are an investigator in Ms. Vasvija Vidovic's office, I take it.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am an investigator in Vasvija Vidovic's office, working on the Oric case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that as part of your duties you research documents, examine archives, interview potential witnesses, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you also coordinate the work of other investigators?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as part of your duties do you request documents from sources, receive those documents, and then file them?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you also on occasion go and inspect archives, make copies of documents, and then file those?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be right that you, you and the team, records -- or keeps records of all documents received, when they were received, and from what source?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There is a very strict procedure, and that's followed in Mrs. Vidovic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, have you for the purposes of testifying today prepared a spreadsheet which sets out the details for all of the Defence exhibits, the source, the date of document, and other details?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I prepared such a spreadsheet and in this spreadsheet there is information from the Defence exhibits to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in preparing it, did you also, when necessary, seek assistance from other members of the Defence team and other investigators?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Other members of the Defence team assisted me in drawing up this spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness already has a copy of that spreadsheet, otherwise I was going to produce it to her. But we have copies for everyone else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't tell you that we have had time to go through it, except -- although we have had a bird's eye view of it, a cursory look at it. We haven't had time to go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We should perhaps provide one copy to the registry, in any event, or however many copies they need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document, which we seem to -- most of us have in any event, starting with D -- well, it's headed "List of the Defence Exhibits," dated 3 July 2005, and it goes from Defence exhibit D304 to D703. Is that the spreadsheet which you have prepared?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the exhibits to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now, is this also a summary of information which you have in your possession? In other words there is -- there is more that could be said about some of these exhibits but you've summarised certain details?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the summaries, and if you wish I can explain the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that in a moment. Firstly I just want to ask you whether you have, in addition to this chart, records of correspondence which you consulted in preparing this spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a separate file. Should any questions be raised I have the correspondence pertaining to all the documents listed in the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask not necessarily at this stage, but with Your Honour's permission if the witness needs to consult the correspondence file, she should be permitted to do so. We're not proposing to exhibit the whole correspondence file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection on our part. Any objection on your part, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll examine very briefly this chart. Hopefully it's self-explanatory, but if you could talk us through the first entry and the different columns going from left to right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I suggest that we put one page on the ELMO. You can take my first page if you need to so the public can follow what's in the first column, second column, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in the interests of proceeding expeditiously, is it right that firstly, the first column sets out the proposed exhibit number, Defence exhibit number, then the next column states which body or individual issued the document; that if there is a reference number, that that would go into the third column; then one obviously has the date of the document and its description. Taking it just up to there, is that a correct summary of how the chart works?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a correct summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we have columns dealing with the ERN numbers. Perhaps for that first -- that first entry you can explain why the ERN number is the same for the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I have here the English ERN and the B/C/S ERN, and they are the same. If we did a translation, we put the same ERN number on the translation to make it identical with the English ERN. Sometimes when we received official translations, we would get one ERN number in English and a different ERN in Bosnian. In this case, the numbers are the same, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally the details are that that was disclosed by the Prosecution and the date is provided there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the disclosure details, including the precise date of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we see from D304 to D505, those exhibits were all disclosed from the Prosecution. When we go from D506 to D513 and also D515 to D520, we see "EDS." Is is correct that that's the electronic disclosure system?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Have you found, for example, D515?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then you're familiar with the electronic disclosure system? You have a give a verbal answer.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We use the EDS, the database available to us, and in that way we arrived at a certain number of documents. And in the column entitled "disclosure details" one can see that these documents were ones we found on the EDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And maybe just skipping back to D514, if you could explain a little bit about that entry because it says "registrar to Ms. Edina Becirevic," so to you. Can you just talk us through that entry and what would have happened in that situation?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: In this case, the exhibit is a set of documents received from the registry of the Hague Tribunal. We had asked access to a certain number of cases which, in our view, were of interest. In August 2003, after having received official approval to travel to The Hague, I searched through some of these files, including the documents from the Krstic case and the documents and exhibits of both the Prosecution and the Defence. This document arrived after I had searched through the Krstic exhibits. I looked at the originals, marked the documents that were of interest to us, and then I would receive copies of them. So the source here is the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So to summarise, one source is the OTP, another source is the electronic disclosure system, another source is the registry?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to take you to some that aren't any none of those sources. If we take you to D528 firstly.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you say D518 or D528?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 528. According to this that's a document from the Official Gazette of the Serbian People, but the source there described as ZK DF BiH and it refers to "Analysis of the Drina Corps." Can you explain that entry to us in a bit more detail.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: In this case the lead counsel, Ms. Vidovic, wrote to the joint command of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina with a specific request that they provide us with an analysis of the Drina Corps. This was not just an analysis but there were also a large number of attachments, maps, and other documents. And after receiving approval, we expected the original documents. The documents were delivered to a Mr. Edin Folan [phoen], Defence investigator, and we have the date when this occurred, and that was the 19th of November, 2003. The document itself is the Official Gazette of the Serbian People, and in column 3 we have the issue 0217/91, and then in the next column is the date of the document, the 24th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in other words the Federation army, the joint command of the Federation army, has its own archives and attached to an analysis they carried out documents, some of which you copied. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: After we had inspected the originals, these documents were photocopied for us in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After we had selected the documents we were interested in, a document about the handover was drawn up with a precise list of the documents that we took over from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was done in every such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if we can go to D582, another source which I want to ask you briefly about. It's actually D582 to D599. There we see "The Institute For the Research of Crimes Against Humanity and International Law" in Sarajevo. Can you explain for us a little bit about what that institute is.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: First maybe I should tell you something about the institute itself. The Institute For the Research of Crimes Against Humanity and International Law in Sarajevo is headed by Professor Smail Cekic who is a historian and teaches at the faculty of political sciences in Sarajevo. This is a very credible institute. It was established in 1992 and as an institute it's part of the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right then that the institute has its own collection of documents and these are -- exhibits are from their collection?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we can look D600 and its reference to the FBiH intelligence service. Could you just explain briefly the procedure which you went through in order to obtain copies of documents from the FBiH intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the intelligence security service of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the FOSS, the procedure was slightly different because we were not able to inspect the original documents. We were only able to look at their catalogues and tell them what documents we are interested in. But they did not permit us, as the other sources did - I'm referring to the army and so on - they did not permit us to enter their premises and inspect the original documents. We simply told them what documents we were interested in. Ms. Vidovic sent an official letter to them, specifying the documents we were interested in, and these documents were later delivered to us but only photocopies of these documents were delivered to us. Of course in this case also, we always asked that a separate list be drawn up, signed by the person issuing the document and the person who had received the document. In this case, it was sent by courier, but the handover was conducted formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you retain the correspondence in relation to those deliveries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever there was a handover of documents, I have a separate file here in which we have a record for every set of documents, and a letter including the request to inspect the documents. And after that, the list of documents we received, the person who handed them over, and the person from our office who received the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally if I could ask you about the documents from D622 onwards of which the source is Mirsad Mustafic to Ms. Edina Becirevic, 12 June 2005 in Tuzla. I'll ask you first of all to tell us who Mirsad Mustafic is.

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: During the war, Mirsad Mustafic was president -- excuse me, a representative of the Serbian municipality with a seat in Tuzla. After the war he kept his private collection of documents. Ms. Vidovic approached him via an official request that, first of all, he allow us to see the originals and then Mr. Mustafic copied the documents and I put together the records concerning the handing over of the documents on the date specified. Could you just remind me what the number was?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. D662 and there -- and following. Are these documents which Mr. Mustafic, as far as you know, retained from having handled during the war in that capacity as a member of the municipal War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the documents that he received in his capacity as the representative of the Srebrenica municipality with the seat in Tuzla. Those were the documents that were -- pertaining to the period when he was officially occupying that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And according to the last column, he personally delivered those documents to you on the 12th of June, 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I won't ask about some of the exhibits where I'm mentioned, because then I might have to give evidence. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask -- in fact, Your Honour, I'm not sure whether we should adopt the procedure which was adopted with the Prosecution, that I now tender these 399 exhibits through this witness because I want to ask for an exhibit number for this spreadsheet or whether that should wait until the conclusion of Mr. Di Fazio's cross-examination. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could do either, but I want to make sure and want confirmation of, Madam Registrar, is in the first page of this spreadsheet where we see the first exhibit showing the number D304, does it reflect the proper sequence of the Defence exhibits that we have so far?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it that the last document that has been filed by the Defence was D303?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So what I suggest, Mr. Jones, is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you proceed with tendering all these documents, and the spreadsheet itself will be exhibit -- Defence Exhibit D704.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And of course the position is reserved for the Prosecution to contest any of these documents, the admissibility of any of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. And I -- just in so far as the numbering, just to let you know, we entirely agree with you and I was going to recommend that myself. It suits us and makes sense, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're happy with that arrangement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. So you may proceed along those lines. And the spreadsheet itself, I don't think this goes with it, the e-mail from Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, that needn't be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That doesn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I should say these exhibits have been already delivered, so I don't ask the witness whether she produces these exhibits to be tendered. I think the form of words already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed in the way which you consider to be the most practical and which causes least confusion in the minds of the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, indeed, in fact, Your Honour, I was proposing to simply tender this witness for cross-examination and I think enough has been said in terms of tendering these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the Defence witness -- Defence has tendered into evidence 400 -- that would be 400 documents, starting with Exhibit Number D304, right up and inclusive of the 703, the 703. The description of each of these documents is contained in the spreadsheet against the number given to each of these documents. And this spreadsheet is also being tendered by the Defence and marked as Defence exhibit D704.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If anyone feels confused with the way I have presented it, please speak out now before it becomes too late. All right. Mr. Di Fazio seems to be happy as well. All right, I think giving Ms. Edina Becirevic for any cross-examination that you may wish to conduct. You've got 17 minutes before we go into break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll be well and truly finished by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam Becirevic, during the course of your evidence, you said that one of the tasks that you completed, amongst other tasks, was researching documents; however, I understand that the thrust of your evidence today is simply that -- this: You essentially were a collator and collector of documents, these documents in particular. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went through the archives, collected, and controlled what other team members did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought as much. Thank you. Would you please look at D431 on your list. Now, that bears a particular ERN number, what is referred to in this institution as an ERN number. Do you see those ERN numbers? They begin with 0207. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know if documents bearing that particular number form part of a collection and has a special name within the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Please allow me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. In fact, I think I can speed things up if I just ask you this. Do you recognise that number as belonging to a class of documents sometimes referred to as the Sokolac collection?

utterances.speaker: EDINA BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's 431, it is a document from the Sokolac collection. That is the only document contained in the spreadsheet from that collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Is there re-examination, which I don't think there is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any questions, Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser? I thought we would have had you for a little bit longer, Madam Becirevic, but I see that you are going to return to your country maybe a little bit earlier. I wish to thank you on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and also on my own behalf for having been kind enough to come over and give testimony on -- in this trial. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom by our usher and you will receive all the attention that you require by the other staff of this Tribunal to facilitate your return back home. On behalf of everyone present here, I thank you once more and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- I saw Mr. Wubben anxious to tell us something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Not anxious, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recall last Friday your request towards Prosecution, that's the issue of the public or confidential label of the 65 ter transcripts. Anyhow, I didn't expect today to have not even one break, because that break would enable me to get my last confirmation with Prosecutor who wasn't present during the course of today. May I take it that I can come back to you first thing tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I can confirm it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. And Mr. Jones had to come back to us on the DVD.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly I was going to come back to you on that and the two other housekeeping matters. As for the DVD, I understood this was a DVD shot on our helicopter ride by the Italians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I gather so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think in fact what I have a DVD by the Caribinari and in fact the Italians weren't on the helicopter. I reviewed the photographs of Tilman and I didn't see the Italians on there. What I have is a DVD with a reconnaissance trip and there is a voiceover in Italian. I wouldn't want that to be an exhibit because I don't speak Italian. On the other hand, there is a PowerPoint presentation which was compiled by the guide which includes photographs -- well, obviously, a number of photographs, but including Rakovici and Bradjevina which there was an issue since we didn't actually travel there ourselves. Having looked at that photograph, I think it could assist and for that to be exhibited. And maybe the whole PowerPoint presentation should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have an objection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Either do we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either do you. So, Madam Registrar, Mr. Tilman will look into this. We have a PowerPoint presentation on CD prepared by Mr. Philip Berikoff that was made available to us prior to the site visit, which we of course went through individually. That will now enter into the evidence together with the CD that contains the photos that Mr. Tilman himself took. If there are others who have got photos that you would like to have inserted in the records, I'm pleased to do that. I myself took quite a few photos. I'm having them put on a CD. If necessary I'll make you copies of it and then you can -- I'm not interested in having a comparative analysis of who is the better photographer between me and Mr. Blumenstock, but if there is anything you would like to keep in the records for the purposes of this case. It is clear to me that the DVD which was made available to us and which I still haven't seen, to be honest with you, if you agree that this was a video taken by the Italian contingent of the Caribinari prior to the site visit or the helicopter flight on which we were, then obviously I don't think we can -- we ought to have it because I wouldn't be so sure that we went and so exactly the same things. I would recognise a good portion of them, but not necessarily everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would rather play it safe and agree with you that it doesn't enter into the records. Any objection to that, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There are two other matters and, I'm sorry, I wouldn't say random but varied. The other matter, and I don't know if it's something that Your Honours can deal with now, but it's something concerning simply the number of witnesses and the length of time which is allocated which is -- and one has in a situation where you have two measurements, you have the question of whether it is the shorter or the longer which counts, and if I can illustrate that by saying by the 14th of September we have finished with our 30 witnesses, can we count on it that we might be able to bring more witnesses in that period. Conversely, if get to 30 September and we're only up to Witness 25, do we try to fit in another five more. The reason I ask is because it's very important for us to figure out how much time we should budget for each witness. Obviously there's an incentive to keep them as brief as possible if it means that it might create space for us to bring other witnesses in. So that's something which we could like your guidance on and we would submit that particularly given what we say is the shortness of time in all sorts of respects, that this should be resolved in favour of the Defence and we should have the benefit of whatever comes later, so in other words 30 witnesses or end of September, whichever comes later. That would be -- if that makes sense. That's one matter which I can just leave with Your Honours for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will discuss it amongst ourselves, obviously, and we will come back to you on this. I don't think there is a point in offering a first reaction to it. It requires thought and we will discuss it and possibly come back to you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That -- in fact, that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that all? Because you said that you had a couple of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, there is another matter and I hesitate in which forum we should raise it you but I will mention it now. Ironically, Your Honour mentioned fees and all of us being paid. In fact for the last two weeks from May onwards we haven't been paid because of the registry system. Nor for any of the work which we did in June have we received fees because of the system run by OLAD. We're challenging that finding, but as far as the summer is concerned, I'm sure as Your Honour can appreciate we're going to be extremely busy during the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But ironically, I think we will be the only party that we won't be receiving any fees for that because the registry's position is that because we're not in court we're not working. It may be at a certain point that guidance from the Trial Chamber would help so we can regulate matters with OLAD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a matter which I can offer you a first reaction. I think out of the three Judges I have got experience of this coming from the past. I encountered this before, and I fully understand the problem, also the predicament in which the parties, Defence in particular, usually finds themselves, in anticipation and during the summer recess, which is not going to be a summer recess at all for them. I won't speak for ourselves because we, too, probably won't have much of a summer recess, as you can imagine. And me, even more, because I will be dealing with other cases, including the issues -- all the joinder applications that there are now pending before this Tribunal, together with Judge Robinson and Judge Liu. So you can imagine what kind of a summer recess we and I in particular are going to have. In this past when this question arose, I did offer my -- not just my understanding but also my services in a way of interceding with the registrar in promoting your submission or any submission that you might have and supporting it, that you will be required to do plenty of work during the summer recess. It may be tied with presence here in The Hague. It has been tied to that in the past in certain instances. What I suggest is the following, that you take the matter up with the registrar. I am going to cut and paste this relative part of the transcript, which you can make use of in your dealings with the registrar. At the same time, we will through the -- our registrar, deputy registrar, communicate with the registrar and OLAD in particular, to confirm our firm conviction that these three weeks that you are going to have between the 23rd of July and the 14th of August you will be required to dedicate in streamlining your defence particularly as a result and in the wake of our decision to "disrupt" - and you are not to take advantage of the word "disrupt" that I'm using now - disrupt your original plan of bringing forward 73 witnesses already with a layout -- laid-out plan. I fully understand that you have got to go through all these 73 witness statements, see what you need to cut off from some of them, see what you are left with, and decide for yourself which will be the 30 best witnesses that you will bring over, being the maximum number. So we will support your -- of course we cannot decide for the registrar. We have no authority to interfere with his discretion; that belongs to him, and him as well. May I also have the reason why you're not being paid -- haven't been paid since May or last week --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was because the trial was scheduled to end, according to the registry's records, by the middle of May and therefore as far as the registry is concerned the Defence aren't entitled to be paid after that date even if the trial continues, unless they can demonstrate compelling reasons -- exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What I will do is I will ask my Senior Legal Officer, please communicate this to him, to try and get the registrar and the head of OLAD to come and see me at my Chambers at the earliest, tomorrow or the day after, at a time which is convenient for the three of us. In the meantime, can I ask you to send us a brief note, it can be done by e-mail, from Mr. Roberts copied, however, to the Prosecution, specifying exactly when this was communicated to you, when you were paid last, and any indication of what the intentions of the registrar are and anticipated payments, when they are anticipated to resume. Because the last thing I want is to have a situation where -- with the approach of the summer recess you have first this suggestion that you will not be paid for three weeks because that's a recess, you're not supposed to be working, and secondly you would also not have been paid in the meantime since I don't know when. So we will look into that matter with the caveat that we will only discuss with the registrar and not in any way interfere with his discretion. However, we will express our preoccupation and our desire that responsible counsel and Defence teams be kept adequately remunerated as we go along and not be paid in hiccups --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much indeed. We appreciate that support and those comments. And we raise it also because of course it's the right of the accused to have legal representation provided to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. If you encounter further problems, please, as long as we are seized of this case, do not hesitate to communicate them to us. And you are also free to raise this matter anywhere else or through the Association of Defence Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nothing else. So I take it you don't have the next witness available to start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 here in Courtroom III, and we will start with witness number 2. Right. Thank you, and good afternoon -- good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of July, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.47 p.m.,
